newsitem.title: INDIA: Mother Teresa's heart problems persist.
newsitem.headline: Mother Teresa's heart problems persist.

text.p: Mother Teresa suffered heart failure for the second time in three days on Sunday, and her doctor said the renowned missionary would not be released from hospital soon.

"Mother Teresa developed heart problems last night and this morning," Dr Dinamani Banerjee, a member of the medical board looking after the 86-year-old Roman Catholic nun at Calcutta's Woodlands Nursing Home, told Reuters.

Mother Teresa, known as the "Saint of the Gutters" for her work with the world's downtrodden, was admitted to hospital with an irregular heart beat early on Friday, the third time since August she had been admitted for emergency care.
She had begun recovering on Saturday and told doctors she wanted to go home.
But Banerjee said the Nobel Peace Prize winner suffered left ventricular heart failure on Saturday night and again on Sunday morning.
"She is more stable than what she was on Thursday night but recurrence of heart failure needs more investigation and we are not releasing her soon," Banerjee said.
The doctor said Mother Teresa was being given oxygen from time to time and her problem had been checked with medication. She was in the intensive cardiac unit but not in critical condition.
"We cannot say there is no danger for her life but at this moment she is not critical," Dr S.K. Sen told reporters, adding that doctors had not been able to reduce her emergency medication.
A hospital medical bulletin said, "Mother is progressing well but her heart failure and irregular beats are still persisting. She needs further observation and investigations."

Sister Mitra, in charge of the cardiac unit at Woodlands Nursing Home, said Mother Teresa had spoken to nuns from her Missionaries of Charity religious order and written a letter before she developed heart problems on Sunday.
Fitted with a heart pacemaker in 1989, Mother Teresa has spent time in hospital for heart disease, bacterial pneumonia, broken ribs, malaria, and lung problems.
She spent nearly three weeks at Woodlands in August and September for heart trouble, malaria and pneumonia.
Two weeks after returning to her Calcutta-based order, she fell off a chair and hit her head. A brain scan revealed a blood clot in the brain. She was released after it disappeared.
Last Saturday, Mother Teresa received honorary American citizenship, one of only five people in U.S. history, in a ceremony led by U.S. Ambassador to India Frank Wisner.
She began her life's work in the slums of Calcutta, India's most densely populated city, in 1949.
